name: Alsea
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 8 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Buckley, Eugene. 2007. Vowel-sonorant metathesis in Alsea. International Journal of American Linguistics 73(1):1-39. ('to appear in IJAL', 84 pp.), the Internet Archive copy of www.ling.upenn.edu/~gene/papers/. Corroborated by Buckley, Eugene. 1989. The structure of the Alsea verb root. University of Oregon Papers in Linguistics 2 (1989 Hokan-Penutian Workshop), 1-17, sec. 3.1.
catalog_locator: Sec. 7.3 'Stress placement', draft pp. 48-49; supporting sec. 7.2 pp. 46-48. Buckley 1989 sec. 3.1.
catalog_quote: Stress in the latest attestation of Alsea also does not appear to be sensitive to weight or syllable structure, but rather is primarily found on either the stem or specific suffixes (such as the inchoative). [...] The resulting pattern is consistent with the usual situation attested in the transcriptions: stress on the root vowel when present, otherwise on a suffixal vowel. Not every token follows this rule — which need not be synchronic at any rate — but it is true for the great majority of cases. [sec. 7.2] These suffixes are nearly always transcribed as stressed by Frachtenberg and Jacobs. [...] in the absence of a stress-attracting suffix such as the inchoative, the short stem is sometimes attested with stress, as in [ɬ-tíms-iyu] 'closed (suddenly)' in (5), phonemically /ɬ-tms-iyu/. It appears that stresses such as this, which do not fall on vowels that are lexically present, are assigned postlexically at the left edge of the word, at which time excrescent (or epenthetic) vowels are available to bear stress. [Buckley 1989 sec. 3.1] Though I have generally not marked it here, the stress most often falls on the root vowel in the long stem and on a suffix — such as the inchoative — in the short stem: tá p-al, tp-áy. This stress pattern is not completely consistent, however, so it does not seem possible to derive the stem alternations from the location of stress.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File checked: (84-pp. Word PDF, created 13 Oct 2005, title page 'VOWEL-SONORANT METATHESIS IN ALSEA, Eugene Buckley, University of Pennsylvania (draft of October 13, 2005, subject to revision; to appear in IJAL)'), plus its extracted text. Both quoted sentences are present verbatim on p. 50 (lines 2239-2261 of): 'Stress in the latest attestation of Alsea also does not appear to be sensitive to weight or syllable structure, but rather is primarily found on either the stem or specific suffixes (such as the inchoative).'.. 'The resulting pattern is consistent with the usual situation attested in the transcrip-tions: stress on the root vowel when present, otherwise on a suffixal vowel. Not ever…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is morphologically governed, not weight- or position-based: it falls on the root (stem) vowel when the stem has one (full/long or heavy stem), and on a suffix vowel when the stem is the vowelless short stem; certain suffixes (inchoative -Vy, transitive irrealis -V?V) are nearly always stressed. Corroborated by Buckley 1989 sec. 3.1: 'stress most often falls on the root vowel in the long stem and on a suffix -- such as the inchoative -- in the short stem: ta.p-al, tp-ay'.
new_statements.exceptions: Pattern 'not completely consistent' (1989) / 'not every token follows this rule' (2007); short stems sometimes stressed on an epenthetic vowel (e.g. [L-ti'ms-iyu] 'closed suddenly'), which Buckley takes to be assigned postlexically at the left edge of the word; clitics generally unstressed but their epenthetic vowel occasionally bears stress (Buckley 1987). Stressed vowels typically transcribed long (Buckley 2020).
new_statements.domain_note: Statement concerns word-level stress as transcribed by Frachtenberg and Jacobs in texts and elicited verb forms (philological corpus; language dormant since 1950s). Buckley speculates an earlier penultimate-stress stage but explicitly as diachronic conjecture.
new_statements.identity_note: Buckley's data are the Alsea dialect proper as recorded by Frachtenberg (1910-13), Jacobs (1935) and Harrington (1942); Yaquina (the other member of alse1251) is attested only in Dorsey's 1884 vocabularies and is not separately described for stress. Statement applies to 'the latest attestation of Alsea', i.e. early-20th-c. Alsea.

sources.note: Sec. 7.3 'Stress placement' (draft pp. 47-48): stress in attested Alsea is not sensitive to weight or syllable structure but is found primarily on the stem or on specific suffixes (e.g. inchoative); usual pattern: stress on the root vowel when present, otherwise on a suffixal vowel; not every token follows this. Also (sec. 7.2) inchoative -Vy and transitive irrealis -V?V suffixes 'nearly always transcribed as stressed'; short (vowelless) stems occasionally carry stress on an epenthetic vowel, assigned postlexically at the left edge. Speculates an earlier penultimate-stress stage.

sources.note: The Glottolog 'description' tag attaching this thesis to Alsea is a misassignment: the work describes West Flemish, Poznań Polish, Central Catalan and Quito Spanish. It says nothing about Alsea word stress. Caveat on completeness: the LingBuzz server closed both downloads (rc 28 then rc 18) so only the first 85 of the thesis pages (front matter, abstract, chapters 1-4 through sec. 4.2) were read; the complete table of contents, which was recovered, lists no chapter on any North American language.
